book: 154 - Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge

chapters.relation: The introduction surveys Doctor Strange's history from Stan Lee and Steve Ditko's 1963 comics to the 2016 Benedict Cumberbatch film, framing him as Marvel's mystic loner defended by Wong and trained by the Ancient One. It previews the book's guiding philosophical questions: how Strange reconciles hard-boiled science with mystical training, why his line about being 'tiny momentary specks within an indifferent universe' was wrong, what his astral self says about mind and body, and why he is always so alone.

chapters.file: ch02 - Part I “YOU’RE JUST ANOTHER TINY, MOMENTARY SPECK WITHIN AN INDIFFERENT UNIVERSE”.md

chapters.relation: Dunn argues that Strange begins as a foot soldier of the Baconian project (Bacon and Descartes' program of conquering nature and treating death as an enemy to be subdued, embodied in his surgical God-complex and neurogenesis research), and that its shipwreck drives him to Kamar-Taj. Using Nietzsche, he reads both Strange and Kaecilius as sick with the 'spirit of revenge against time' — Kaecilius fleeing into Dormammu's timeless Dark Dimension as Nietzsche's Hinterweltler, Strange clinging to his unrecoverable past. The climactic 'Dormammu, I've come to bargain' time loop is interpreted as Nietzsche's eternal return weaponized, and Strange's 'Pain's an old friend' as his achievement of amor fati, echoing the Ancient One's dying claim that death is what gives life meaning.

chapters.file: ch04 - Death Gives Meaning to Life.md
chapters.relation: Lee reads Strange's car crash as Heideggerian angst and the Call of conscience that ends his 'ontic' life of treating patients as reputation-building problems, forcing a choice between authenticity and a mask. Kaecilius and Dormammu embody the inauthentic flight from death (Kaecilius going 'beyond good and evil' Nietzsche-style), while the Ancient One's confession — drawing on the Dark Dimension only until Strange could replace her, then stretching one moment into a thousand to watch the snow — models accepting mortality. Dormammu's torment in Strange's time loop is compared to Camus's Sisyphus, supporting the thesis that without an ending life is endless repetition, so 'death gives meaning to life.'

Cleary reads Strange as a would-be Nietzschean Übermensch — brilliant, striving, and flirting with nihilism via the 'tiny momentary speck' line — whose narcissism, not his ideals, blocks both self-overcoming and love. Strange's rage at Christine Palmer's wine and cheese ('don't pity me') is explained through Nietzsche's attack on pity as herd morality, and his fixation on restoring his old surgeon-self as refusing Zarathustra's call to burn oneself to ashes. The Ancient One leaving him to die on Everest, Mordo's hard training, and Wong refusing to laugh at his jokes exemplify Nietzschean friendship as challenge and 'war,' culminating in the 'shared higher thirst for an ideal above them' that lets Strange overcome himself.

chapters.file: ch06 - The Existential Redefinition of Doctor Strange.md
chapters.relation: DiGeorgio traces Strange's 'existential conversion' from scientific nihilism ('matter and nothing more') through Sartrean bad faith — playing the brilliant surgeon while not really believing life meaningless, refusing the Ancient One's widened keyhole — to authenticity. His hesitation to stay and fight after killing a zealot, and the Ancient One's 'it's not about you,' set up his choice to defend humanity as Sartre's universal decree, choosing for all humankind in anguish and freedom. The endless time loop imposed on Dormammu is read as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence demanding total commitment to one's choices, so that by the end Strange lives existence-precedes-essence: what he does, not his 'brilliant surgeon' essence, defines him.

chapters.file: ch07 - Part II “FORGET EVERYTHING THAT YOU THINK YOU KNOW”.md

chapters.relation: Boudreaux maps Strange's comic-book journey into the Orb of Agamotto (dragged in by the Silver Dagger, greeted by a hookah-smoking caterpillar, tempted by counterfeit heroes like the Silver Surfer and Hulk) onto Descartes's Meditations. Empiricism (Locke's tabula rasa, Hume's sense-data) collapses when the senses are so thoroughly deceived inside the Orb, and innate ideas plus the Law of Non-Contradiction are not enough, so Strange reasons his way to the cogito — 'Nothing merits belief here — except oneself!' — just as Descartes doubts the evil demon. The caterpillar is revealed as Agamotto, playing the role of Descartes's non-deceiving God whose guidance lets Strange escape, and Strange's astral projections are offered as dramatic proof of mind-body dualism.

Manninen applies virtue epistemology — built on Aristotle's virtue ethics and golden mean — to the four students of the Ancient One, asking not what they knew of the mystic arts but how they knew it. Strange's photographic memory exemplifies reliabilist epistemic ability, while Montmarquet's responsibilist virtues (impartiality, intellectual courage) are measured against Pangborn's self-serving magic, Kaecilius's courage without impartiality, and Mordo's epistemic rigidity and blind deference to authority ('no more questions'), each a vice of excess or deficiency. The Book of Cagliostro frames Wong's 'no knowledge in Kamar-Taj is forbidden, only certain practices,' and Strange emerges closest to the balanced intellectual character, though Aristotle demands consistency, not a single virtuous act.

Timm argues Strange follows Socrates' path from arrogance to Socratic heroism: the hand injury forces intellectual humility (the Oracle-at-Delphi moment), the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor and astral-form lesson ('to show you just how much you don't know') enact the Socratic method of questioning the supposedly wise, and the astral projection is literally the examined life — Socrates' unexamined life not worth living. Strange's commitment to protecting humanity from interdimensional evil parallels the gadfly who risks death to improve Athens, his refusal to do injustice even under pressure echoes the Crito, and his repeated willingness to die for others (facing Dormammu, holding the Shambler back) completes the Socratic Hero profile.

chapters.file: ch11 - We Can All Be Socratics Supreme.md
chapters.relation: Pape uses the Ancient One's keyhole metaphor to argue that all knowledge is partial and biased: Bacon's confident scientific method ('human knowledge and human power meet in one') is itself just a useful belief, while Socratic awareness of one's ignorance — knowing that you have blind spots, even if you cannot see them — is the real wisdom. She reads the film's running gags as bias lessons (the 'Mister Doctor' exchange, Strange mistaking the wifi password 'Shamballa' for a mantra, the noble-savage prejudice) and feminist critiques of impartiality as itself partial. The whitewashing controversy around Tilda Swinton's Ancient One — weighed against the Fu Manchu stereotype of the 1963 comics and Iron Man 3's Mandarin-as-Trevor-Slattery subversion — shows how filmmakers can confront the biases they cannot simply remove.

chapters.file: ch12 - I Control It by Surrendering Control.md
chapters.relation: Pérez stages the film's natural-law debate through Ayn Rand's Objectivism (Steve Ditko's avowed influence): Mordo's absolutism — 'there is no other way,' 'the bill comes due' — mirrors the axioms of existence, consciousness, and identity (A is A), with Cicero and Aquinas' divinely eternal natural law as the older backdrop. Rand's system is strained by the film's events: Wong dies and is un-died when Strange rolls back time in Hong Kong, and the Eye of Agamotto's time loop creates three simultaneous realities, so 'A' is no longer self-evidently one thing. The chapter concludes that Strange, exercising exactly the Objectivist freedom to think and choose, violates natural law in order to uphold it — sacrificing himself Prometheus- or Sisyphus-like in the Dormammu bargain — while Mordo's departure is wounded pride rather than principle.

chapters.file: ch13 - Part III “REALITY IS ONE OF MANY”.md

chapters.relation: Kowalski reads the film's astral-form scenes as a dramatization of Cartesian substance dualism against Strange's opening physicalism ('There is no such thing as spirit! We are made of matter and nothing more'): the Ancient One pushing his astral body out refutes physicalism, his soul reads books while his body sleeps, and he fights Kaecilius's acolyte as a visible astral form in Christine Palmer's ER. The chapter then confronts the classic interaction problem — Descartes' pineal gland and 'animal spirits,' Elisabeth of Bohemia's and Garrett Thomson's objections — asking how an immaterial astral form can turn pages or knock over vending machines, joking that it would take 'a very strange form of interactionism.' The Ancient One's account of magic as energy drawn from other dimensions of the multiverse is offered as the film's own dualist reply, with a closing plea for the epistemic humility Strange had to learn.

chapters.file: ch15 - One Thing We Know Is That Life Is Strange.md
chapters.relation: Donovan and Richardson read Jason Aaron and Chris Bachalo's 2015 comic run as portraying Strange as a natural philosopher-scientist: he researches the Book of Vishanti to trap Zelma Stanton's mind maggots, combines inductive and deductive reasoning, and must eventually write new laws of magic when the old books fail. Aristotle's four causes and teleology are applied concretely — Strange spares the Een'Gawori slugs because their end or purpose is merely to consume magic (acorns cannot be conquerors), letting him deduce something else destroyed their homeworld — with Aquinas credited for mediating Aristotle to Christendom. Lord Imperator and the Empirikul embody a fanatical, inquisitional 'science' (draining magic from Fandazar Foo and the Sanctum, unleashing the Thing in the Cellar), contrasted with the genuinely entwined history of science, philosophy, and magic from Copernicus, Bacon, Galileo, and Kepler through Descartes and Newton to quantum 'spooky action' — Clarke's law that advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.

Latta reads the film through Bergson's distinction between clock time and duration: Strange is introduced as pure quantitative multiplicity — identifying Chuck Mangione's 'Feels So Good' (1977) mid-surgery, surrounding himself with watches, including Christine Palmer's inscribed 'Time will tell how much I love you' — while the Ancient One lives duration, surrendering to the river's current. Kaecilius embodies 'chronological nihilism' ('time is an insult'), and his and Dormammu's timeless Dark Dimension is existentially impossible for Bergson, since life only progresses and endures in time. The climax shows Strange recreating the present in the endless looped bargain with Dormammu ('pain is an old friend'), growing through qualitative multiplicity and élan vital, until the shattered watch — hands broken, inscription intact — marks his conversion from counting time to living it.

holes.name: Ayn Rand
holes.what: Twentieth-century Russian-American philosopher of Objectivism, an egoist ethics of rational self-interest and laissez-faire capitalism expressed in novels like The Fountainhead.
holes.why: Chapter 12's entire argument frames Mordo's absolutism and Strange's choice through Rand's Objectivism, noting Steve Ditko's Rand-influenced creation of Doctor Strange.

holes.name: Objectivism (A is A)
holes.what: Rand's philosophy built on three self-evident axioms — existence, consciousness, and identity (the Law of Identity, 'A is A') — with reason as man's means of survival.
holes.why: Chapter 12 tests each axiom against Wong's death-and-reanimation and Strange's multiverse of simultaneous realities, arguing the film breaks Rand's system from the inside.

holes.name: Physicalism
holes.what: The metaphysical view that human persons are nothing over and above their working physical parts, with all mental facts explainable by physical (brain) facts.
holes.why: Chapter 14 casts Strange's 'we are made of matter and nothing more' creed as physicalism set against the Ancient One's substance dualism, with the astral-form scenes as its cinematic refutation.
